# The sentence a load bank file may support

> **Direct Answer Block**: The exact bounded engineering sentence a 5-pass liquid load bank flash report can legally support—and why a rack test never certifies whole-hall seasonal redundancy. In mission-critical data center commissioning and operations, engineers enforce this boundary using deterministic physical equations, calibrated field instrumentation, and auditable sign-off gates rather than relying on vendor brochure summaries, uncalibrated software plots, or verbal assurances. Every measurement and state transition must be recorded with synchronized UTC timestamps and explicit pass/fail thresholds before a signature is granted.

![The file supports one sentence, or none.](figures/flagship/fig-04-sampling-and-stale-data.png)

After the checks, you get one sentence, or you get none. The sentence names the channels that were live, the clock used, the dwell that was actually met, the sign of the heat, and where the heat went. It does not say the hall passed, the CDU is accepted, or the IT may arrive.

If any check failed, the sentence is that the file is not a valid test, with the reason left in those terms. That is a useful result. Hiding it under a kinder heading is how the next meeting quotes a pass you did not have.

Scope is part of the sentence. A valid file on one loop is not a valid file on the hall. If the signature page is wider than the loops that were judged, strike the extra words. Do not add them back in the executive summary.

Hand that sentence, not the plot, to the verification close-out. A curve without the sentence is a picture. Pictures get filed. They do not get signed as proof.

---

## 1. First-Principles Engineering Formulation and Governing Mathematics

In high-density data center environments, verbal summaries and qualitative status tiles routinely obscure incipient physical failures. Whether auditing a $120\,\text{kW}$ liquid-cooled rack boundary, evaluating a 1-second telemetry time series, or verifying plant redundancy prior to handover, the governing physical relationship for this protocol is expressed as:

$$\text{Enthalpy Closure} = \left[ 1 - \frac{|P_{\text{elec}} - (Q_{\text{liquid}} + Q_{\text{air}})|}{P_{\text{elec}}} \right] \times 100\% \ge 97.0\%$$

When any term on the left-hand or right-hand side of this relationship is left unmeasured, inferred from an uncalibrated nameplate, or averaged across an unverified time window, the resulting engineering record cannot support a valid operational signature. Field engineers must verify each physical variable independently using NIST/ISO 17025 traceable instruments before proceeding to the next gate in the sequence.

| Audit Verification Parameter | Unacceptable / Defective Field Practice | Auditable First-Principles Requirement | Mandatory Action on Failure |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Boundary Definition** | Implied by vendor brochure or slide deck | Explicitly bounded on stamped P&ID / SLD with tag IDs | Halt acceptance; issue formal boundary clarification |
| **Measurement & Telemetry Proof** | Single uncalibrated display reading or 60-sec average | Calibrated Class A/0.5S sensor with 1-sec UTC timestamp | Reject dataset; classify point as `0x40` Stale or `0x80` Bad |
| **Pass / Fail Acceptance Gate** | Qualitative "Looks OK" or "Within Normal Range" | Quantitative numerical corridor cited from revision in force | Log Category A/B defect; withhold retainage or permit |
| **Custody & Sign-Off Record** | Single bundled "Accepted" signature at end of meeting | Scoped, dated sentence naming exact proved & unproved lines | Strike unsupported claims; issue Conditional Refusal |

---

## 2. Deep-Dive Technical Protocol and Field Implementation

The following field protocol—adapted directly from **Volume 02: *Read and Use Load Bank Data: A Field Guide to the Flash Report***—establishes the step-by-step verification mechanics required on the data hall floor:

A liquid load bank is not an island, and a commissioning test does not occur in an abstract vacuum. The load bank connects directly to live facility infrastructure: to a Coolant Distribution Unit (CDU), to an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) or automatic transfer switch (ATS), and to computer room air handlers (CRAH).

A frequent failure mode in commissioning reporting is the confusion of boundaries:
- When a facility CDU circulating pump trips on an internal inverter fault, an inexperienced team may blame the load bank for "failing to maintain flow."
- Conversely, when a load bank's high-temperature safety switch trips due to poorly submerged heating elements, a vendor may attempt to blame the facility CDU for "running too warm."

The flash report must draw an uncompromising physical and operational boundary between the load bank (the machine under test) and the external facility gear (the host environment). A failure of external facility gear is an operational event; it is not automatically a failure of the load bank. But it must be documented with absolute precision so that the true cause of an interrupted dwell is transparent to any future auditor.

## The four external gear lines

The flash report includes an External Gear section with four explicit lines, evaluated before, during, and after every test run:

### Line 1: Coolant Distribution Unit (CDU)
The CDU is responsible for circulating secondary coolant through the load bank and transferring heat to the primary facility chilled water loop via its internal brazed plate or shell-and-tube heat exchanger.

The flash report monitors four CDU interface metrics:
- **Secondary Loop Supply Temperature (T_CDU,sup)**: The temperature of fluid exiting the CDU heat exchanger before entering the load-bank supply manifold. The report verifies that the CDU maintains its declared supply setpoint (e.g., 35.0°C ± 1.0 K). If the primary facility water warms up, causing T_CDU,sup to drift upward to 42.0°C, that drift is recorded as a **CDU boundary condition excursion**, not as a load-bank heating error.
- **Secondary Delivery Pressure & Pump Curve**: The available static pressure delivered by the CDU pumps at rated cluster flow. If the CDU pump speed hunts or cavitates due to poor suction pressure, the resulting flow fluctuations are logged against the CDU line.
- **CDU Approach Temperature**: The temperature difference between the secondary return fluid and the primary facility water (Approach = T_sec,ret - T_pri,sup). An increasing approach temperature over time indicates fouling in the CDU heat exchanger plates, not element degradation in the load bank.

### Line 2: Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) & Automatic Transfer Switch (ATS)
The electrical power feeding the load bank originates from facility distribution switchboards, often backed by static UPS modules or diesel generator ATS gear.

The flash report monitors:
- **Voltage Stability & Harmonic Distortion**: Line voltage sag during full-load staging. If the facility transformer sags from 415V down to 380V under full 480kW load, the active power of resistive elements will drop by nearly 16% ($P \propto V²$). The report must document that the load drop was driven by facility utility sag, not by early contactor shedding.
- **ATS Transfer Immunity**: If an integrated system test (IST) initiates an upstream power transfer, the duration of the open-transition interruption must be timed. If the interruption exceeds the load bank's 24VDC control buffer hold-up time (typically 40ms), the unit will de-energize safely, which must be attributed to the facility transfer transient.

### Line 3: Power Distribution Units (PDUs) and Busways
The physical power path from the electrical panelboard through busway tap-off boxes and drop cables to the load-bank terminals:
- **Terminal Temperature Rise (ΔT_terminal)**: Infrared thermography or calibrated thermocouple monitoring of cable lugs and contactor terminals. Terminal temperature must not exceed 70°C (or the specific rating of the 90°C RHW-2 conductor).
- **Busway Voltage Drop**: Voltage drop across the temporary feeder cables must be bounded at ≤ 2.0%.

### Line 4: Computer Room Air Handlers (CRAH / CRAC / Fan Wall)
The facility air-handling units responsible for absorbing the 16% to 20% companion air sensible heat dissipated by the load-bank blowers:
- **Intake/Discharge Air Differential**: Verifying that the data hall's hot-aisle containment (HAC) maintains proper negative pressure relative to the cold aisle, preventing thermal recirculation into adjacent server rows.
- **CRAH Chilled Water Valve Response**: Confirming that CRAH cooling coils modulate open smoothly in response to the companion air load without overflowing condensate drain pans.

## How to write an honest boundary sentence

When an anomaly or interruption occurs during a test run, the Recorder must write an honest boundary sentence. 

An honest boundary sentence adheres to three strict grammatical rules:
1. **It names the exact physical parameter that breached a threshold.**
2. **It names the specific side of the boundary where the breach occurred.**
3. **It states the consequence on the test scene without assigning speculative blame.**

### Example of an Honest Boundary Sentence
> *"At 15:42:18 UTC, during Step 4 (120kW dwell), secondary coolant supply temperature from the facility CDU rose to 39.8°C (exceeding the cited pretest boundary of 36.5°C). The load bank maintained rated electrical load (120.1kW) and normal flow (176.4 LPM), but return temperature reached 49.9°C, triggering an automated overtemperature supervisory alarm. The dwell was halted at Minute 11 by operator command. Verdict for Step 4: INVALID due to facility CDU supply temperature excursion; load bank electrical and hydraulic tracking remained fully compliant."*

### Example of a Dishonest Sentence
> *"The test had some issues with the building water, but the load bank basically passed."*

The dishonest sentence provides zero data, cites no timestamp, names no temperature, and attempts to claim an illegitimate pass. An auditor will reject it instantly. The honest sentence provides exact numbers, identifies the CDU boundary excursion, records the aborted dwell, and preserves the technical integrity of the load-bank hardware for the re-test.

## External gear pass/fail status

On the flash report summary sheet, each of the four external gear lines is given an independent status:
- **NORMAL**: Operated within the cited design envelope for the entire run.
- **EXCURSION**: Breached an operating envelope, with exact timestamps and affected parameters documented.
- **NOT APPLICABLE (N/A)**: Gear was excluded from the testing boundary by pre-declared agreement.

A facility CDU excursion does not ruin the reputation of a well-engineered load bank, nor does a clean load bank excuse a failing facility plant. The report records both, in daylight, separated by the physical manifold boundary.

---

## 3. Field Verification Checklist and Instrumentation Hygiene

To execute this protocol without introducing measurement bias or scope ambiguity, the responsible engineer enforces four mandatory field rules:
1. **Instrument Traceability Before Observation**: Verify that every thermometer (4-wire Pt100 RTD Class A), pressure transducer ($\le \pm 0.1\%$ span), flowmeter, balometer, or power analyzer carries a current calibration certificate and passes a pre-test zero/span check on the day of the walk.
2. **Synchronized Time-Series Capture**: Align all digital loggers and gateway pollers to a single UTC reference clock (via IEEE 1588v2 PTP at $\pm 1\,\text{ms}$ for electrical Sequence of Events, or NTP at $\pm 10\,\text{ms}$ for thermal/hydraulic dwells). Never merge unsynchronized CSV files by row index.
3. **Explicit Isolation of Disturbances vs. Control Handles**: Hold upstream supply temperatures, parallel cabinet loads, and containment door states constant during the observation dwell so that transient plant drift is never mistaken for steady-state equipment performance.
4. **Written Record Prior to Signature**: Record every boundary tag, measured value, uncertainty tolerance, and open limitation in ink on the controlled project sheet before leaving the equipment line-up.

## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

### Why does "The sentence a load bank file may support" matter during high-density data center commissioning and operations?
The exact bounded engineering sentence a 5-pass liquid load bank flash report can legally support—and why a rack test never certifies whole-hall seasonal redundancy. When project teams bypass this rule to meet a commercial schedule milestone, unverified physical assumptions—such as hidden hydraulic pressure drops, unlogged polling gaps, unblanked bypass leakage, or uncalibrated sensor offsets—transfer directly into live 24/7 production as latent single points of failure.

### How do you quantitatively verify compliance with "load bank flash report acceptance verdict" on the physical floor?
Compliance is verified by executing the governing mathematical balance ($$\text{Enthalpy Closure} = \left[ 1 - \frac{|P_{\text{elec}} - (Q_{\text{liquid}} + Q_{\text{air}})|}{P_{\text{elec}}} \right] \times 100\% \ge 97.0\%$$) using independent, calibrated field instruments across a stabilized steady-state dwell window (minimum 15 to 30 minutes for thermal and hydraulic systems), and confirming that the discrepancy between primary and secondary measurements remains strictly within the pre-declared acceptance band.

### What should an engineer do if a contractor or vendor submits a report that violates this protocol?
The reviewing engineer must refuse to sign the broad acceptance sentence, mark the specific line item as **Unproved / Defective** on the official audit sheet, and either require a witnessed re-test under a corrected script or isolate the unproved scope under a time-bounded Conditional Acceptance with a $150\%$ to $200\%$ financial retainage escrow holdback.

# Approve the test script before the day

> **Direct Answer Block**: Why every liquid cooling commissioning script must be frozen, version-controlled, and signed with explicit pass/fail bounds before test day begins. In mission-critical data center commissioning and operations, engineers enforce this boundary using deterministic physical equations, calibrated field instrumentation, and auditable sign-off gates rather than relying on vendor brochure summaries, uncalibrated software plots, or verbal assurances. Every measurement and state transition must be recorded with synchronized UTC timestamps and explicit pass/fail thresholds before a signature is granted.

![Approve the expected result before the window.](figures/flagship/fig-01-cx-gate-ladder.png)

A script is a set of steps with an expected result, a stop, and a revision, approved before the window. A script written during the window to match what the plant did is a diary. Diaries do not support a certificate.

The expected result comes from the specification then in force, or from a limit the owner wrote and can point to. It does not come from the first calm hour. If the expected result cell is blank, do not start. Blank is not "use engineering judgment on the night." Judgment on the night is how a pass line moves.

Say who witnesses and who may accept a document instead. Those are different verbs. A letter that a setting was adjusted is not a witnessed changeover. If you did not witness every line, say what was sampled. "We saw enough" is not a sampling rule.

Stops belong in the script, not in someone's memory. The stop is the first safe state, not a root cause. You will not know the cause in the first minute. Writing one there is how the report inherits a guess.

$$\forall \text{Step } k: \quad \text{Script}_k = \{\text{Precondition}, \text{Action}, \text{Pass Band } [L_k, U_k], \text{Abort Trigger}\}$$

## 2. Deep-Dive Technical Protocol and Field Implementation

The following field protocol—adapted directly from **Volume 03: *Finish a Liquid Cooling Verification: Seven Sheets for One Load-Bank Test***—establishes the step-by-step verification mechanics required on the data hall floor:

No dynamic commissioning test may be executed from memory or oral instructions. A test conducted without a pre-approved, step-by-step test script is merely an informal equipment demonstration. It cannot support an engineering completion certificate.

A script that the testing team drafted but which the Owner’s Project Engineer has not formally reviewed and signed is merely an internal working document. It carries no contractual authority. Executing against an unapproved draft leaves the testing team fully exposed to commercial disputes and legal liability if an equipment failure occurs.

**COMMISSIONING DOCUMENT HIERARCHY**

| 1. CODES & STANDARDS | ASHRAE 0-2019, ASHRAE 90.4, NFPA 70, IEC 60364, BSRIA BG 29. |
| :--- | :--- |
| 2. CONTRACT SPECIFICATIONS & BOD | CSI Div 23 & 26, Owner Project Requirements, As-Built P&IDs. |
| 3. COMMISSIONING PLAN (Cx Plan) | Governance rules, level gates, witness protocols, schedules. |
| 4. FUNCTIONAL TEST PROCEDURES (FPT) | Pre-approved, step-by-step scripts with exact numeric bands. |
| 5. MASTER FIELD SHEETS (INK LOGS) | Floor records signed in ink; raw time-series sensor files. |

## The Anatomy of an Auditable Test Script

Every Functional Test Procedure (FPT) and Integrated System Test (IST) script must be structured with consistent, auditable engineering sections:

1. **Test Scope and Boundary**: The specific mechanical and electrical components under test, and the exact physical boundary separating them from adjacent operational equipment.
2. **Governing Reference Documents**: Direct citations of the governing P&ID revision, electrical single-line diagram (SLD), and equipment submittals. Every tolerance must reference a specific contract clause or manufacturer standard; an acceptance tolerance with no cited source is merely an unverified opinion.
3. **Instrumentation and Calibration Schedule**: The specific instrument classes, serial numbers, and calibration certificate IDs required to execute the procedure.
4. **Prerequisite Verification Gate**: Written verification that all preceding level requirements (such as static uncrating, de-energized megger checks, and hydrostatic pressure holds) are fully signed off.
5. **Safety Controls and Environmental Boundaries**: Mandatory Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), arc-flash boundary definitions, spill containment staging, and verified emergency stop paths.
6. **Step-by-Step Execution Sequence**: A sequential table detailing every manual action, the exact physical feedback to observe, the expected numerical tolerance band, and dedicated sign-off cells for measured data and witness initials.
7. **Explicit Stop Conditions**: Clear operational limits that mandate an immediate test halt if breached (such as secondary coolant temperature exceeding 45.0°C, secondary pressure dropping below 100 kPa, or supply phase voltage unbalance exceeding 2.0%).

**STANDARD TEST SCRIPT STEP STRUCTURE**

| STEP | ACTION COMMAND | EXPECTED PHYSICAL RESULT | ACCEPTANCE BAND | MEASURE | SIGN / TIME |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 4.2 | Ramp Load Bank to 50% (Step 2: 600 kW total) Dwell: 45 minutes | Active power stabilizes Secondary supply T increases Heat balance closure ratio | 600 kW +/- 1.5% 36.0°C +/- 0.5°C 97.0% to 101.5% | [ ] [ ] [ ] | Init: ____ Time: ____ Sheet 3 ref |

## Freezing Script Revisions on the Floor

The Commissioning Kickoff Meeting establishes the specific approval status required before a script may be executed on the floor. Only scripts bearing the formal status stamp **"APPROVED FOR EXECUTION - REV [X]"** are permitted in the data hall.

If during testing the mechanical plant exhibits unexpected dynamics that the approved script did not anticipate, modifying the script on the floor with a pencil note is strictly prohibited. Uncontrolled redlining allows the test procedure to quietly adapt to whatever the plant happens to do.

When a procedural modification is necessary:
- The Test Lead pauses the test.
- A formal Engineering Change Notice (ECN) is drafted documenting the deviation, its technical justification, and the amended steps.
- The ECN is signed by the Test Lead, the Contractor Lead, and the Owner’s Project Engineer.
- The script revision is incremented (e.g., Rev 1.0 to Rev 1.1) and re-issued.

If the owner refuses the ECN, testing resumes under the original script, and the failure of the plant to meet the original expected result is logged on the master punch list.

## The Mandatory Script Suite for a High-Density Liquid Hall

A complete verification campaign requires a comprehensive suite of distinct, standalone scripts. Attempting to combine multiple operational verifications into a single high-level procedure produces an unwieldy document that inevitably glosses over critical safety and performance checks.

The verification campaign requires nine dedicated test scripts:

### Phase 1: Static Pre-Start Checklists (Level 2 / Level 3)
- **Script 01: Physical Uncrating, Alignment & Visual QA**: Verification of load-bank chassis integrity, hose routing, fitting seals, and seismic tie-downs.
- **Script 02: De-Energized Electrical Megger & Phase Rotation**: Insulation resistance testing (≥ 100 MΩ at 1000V DC), ground continuity (≤ 0.1 Ω), and confirmation of clockwise A-B-C phase sequence.
- **Script 03: Secondary Loop Flushing, Hydrostatic Hold & Air Purge**: Chemical flushing velocity verification (≥ 1.5 m/s per BSRIA BG 29/2020), hydrostatic pressure hold (1.5× working pressure for 2 hours with zero decay), and automatic deaeration.

### Phase 2: Single-System Functional Testing (Level 4 FPT)
- **Script 04: Autonomous CDU Startup, Flow & Pressure Baseline**: Verification of canned pump VFD ramp profiles, manual differential-pressure setpoint tracking, and cold system resistance.
- **Script 05: CDU N+1 Pump Failover & Autonomous Control**: Physical tripping of the primary pump VFD; verification of standby pump auto-start within < 1.5 s with zero loop cavitation.
- **Script 06: Alarm Injection & Point-to-Point Telemetry**: Physical injection of simulated faults (secondary low flow, expansion tank low level, leak detection rope wetting) and cross-checking BMS telemetry against local instrumentation.

### Phase 3: Integrated System Testing (Level 5 IST)
- **Script 07: Cold No-Heat Baseline Pump Curve**: Hydraulic head versus flow profiling across 4 manual valve throttling points with automated VFD control locked off.
- **Script 08: Multi-Tier Thermal Heat Ladder & Overload Dwell**: Stepped thermal execution (25%, 50%, 75%, 100% full design load, and 110% overload margin) with minimum 45-minute dwells and a 4-hour full-load soak.
- **Script 09: Dynamic Transient Failure & Emergency Shutdown**: 2N primary power feed cut, facility chilled water loss ride-through, and controlled de-energization shutdown sequence.

## The "One Script, One Signature" Principle

Every script in the suite stands as an independent contractual document with its own dedicated sign-off block. Combining a successful cold pump curve and a failed thermal overload step into a single combined signature creates a fundamentally ambiguous record.

Each script must produce its own unambiguous verdict: **PASS**, **FAIL**, or **NOT EXECUTED**. Any unresolved failure within a script immediately generates an entry in the master Issues Log.

# Close-out is not a heat-test report: First-Principles Data Center Engineering Protocol

> **Direct Answer Block**: The seven mandatory deliverables required in a liquid cooling verification closeout binder—beyond a single thermal load bank chart. In mission-critical data center commissioning and operations, engineers enforce this boundary using deterministic physical equations, calibrated field instrumentation, and auditable sign-off gates rather than relying on vendor brochure summaries, uncalibrated software plots, or verbal assurances. Every measurement and state transition must be recorded with synchronized UTC timestamps and explicit pass/fail thresholds before a signature is granted.

![Close-out is the pages, not the curves.](figures/flagship/fig-02-cdu-hydraulic-pandid.png)

The heat window can be honest and still not be turnover. Turnover is the later signature, after the punch on the levels you actually ran is closed, and after you have written which levels you did not run. A photograph album of curves is not that signature.

The short pack a stranger should be able to read without calling you: the sentence, proved or not, or proved only for the systems named. Outstanding work on the next page, even if the page says none. The level map, including levels you refused. What you witnessed and what you accepted as a document. The file judgment, not a kinder summary. The printed punch. The operator pages: tested, not tested, stops, deviations still in force.

An empty tab with a hopeful title is a false document. Seasonal tests, fire integration, and the rest of a full building report belong only if this project ran them. Pretending to have the long list is the same sin as the wrong level certificate.

Training, if you claim operators can run it, is a signature that they were shown those pages. A slide deck is not the signature.

## 2. Deep-Dive Technical Protocol and Field Implementation

The following field protocol—adapted directly from **Volume 03: *Finish a Liquid Cooling Verification: Seven Sheets for One Load-Bank Test***—establishes the step-by-step verification mechanics required on the data hall floor:

A successful thermal heat test is not a facility turnover. Demobilizing load banks from a data hall merely signifies that dynamic verification has concluded. The formal transition of the facility from construction into live IT operations occurs under **Level 6 Close-Out, Turnover, and Operations Handover**.

A turnover certificate signed while punch list items remain unresolved or before the final commissioning report is audited is legally defective. Level 6 turnover is the formal milestone where the Facility Owner, the General Contractor, and the Commissioning Authority collectively certify that the mechanical, electrical, and control systems satisfy the Owner's Project Requirements and are safe to receive high-density compute infrastructure.

**LEVEL 6 TURNOVER DOCUMENT ARCHITECTURE**

| 01 | EXECUTIVE SUMMARY & VERIFIED CLAIM STATEMENT | The signed claim sentence, final project verdict, and summary of operational thermal capacity demonstrated. |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 02 | SCOPE BOUNDARIES & EXCLUSION LETTERS | Explicit scope letters documenting unexecuted levels, seasonal deferred testing, and third-party systems out. |
| 03 | MASTER MILESTONE CERTIFICATES | Formal signed completion certificates for Levels 2, 3, 4, 5. |
| 04 | THE SEVEN SIGNED MASTER SHEETS | Sheets 1 through 7, fully executed, logged in ink, signed. |
| 05 | INSTRUMENT CALIBRATION LOG | Traceable ISO 17025 calibration certificates for all tools. |
| 06 | TIME-SERIES DATA REPOSITORY | Complete raw CSV logs, BMS trend exports, cryptographic SHA. |
| 07 | RESOLVED ISSUES REGISTER | Master Punch List showing 100% Cat 1 & Cat 2 items closed. |
| 08 | SYSTEMS MANUAL SUPPLEMENT | As-tested pump curves, operating bands, fail-safe setpoints. |
| 09 | OPERATIONS TRAINING RECORDS | Witnessed sign-off of facility staff SOP walkthrough. |

## Structure of the Final Commissioning Report

The Final Commissioning Report is the permanent engineering baseline of the liquid cooling infrastructure. Decades later, when the facility undergoes retrofits or failure investigations, engineering teams will refer to this report to verify initial operating parameters.

The report must be compiled with nine standardized sections:

### 1. Executive Summary and Certified Claim
Opens with the exact, unedited claim sentence formulated in Chapter 1. It provides an unambiguous operational summary: the total thermal capacity verified (e.g., 1.2 MW continuous), the primary cooling supply conditions, secondary flow balance metrics, and the formal certification that all tested systems operated within specification.

### 2. Scope Boundaries and Formal Exclusion Letters
A rigorous definition of boundaries. If Level 0 design review or Level 1 factory testing were excluded from the contract, the formal Scope Exclusion Letters signed by the owner must be embedded here. If seasonal testing (such as maximum summer ambient chiller stress testing) must be deferred to a later date, the Deferred Testing Protocol and scheduled execution date are formally documented.

### 3. Master Milestone Completion Certificates
Formal certificate pages for Level 2 (Receipt QA), Level 3 (PFC and Start-Up), Level 4 (Single-System FPT), and Level 5 (Integrated System IST). Each certificate must bear the ink signatures of the Commissioning Lead, Electrical PE, Mechanical PE, Contractor Executive, and Owner’s Authorized Representative.

### 4. The Seven Master Field Sheets
The completed, physical field record sheets (Sheets 1 through 7 from Chapter 16), scanned in full color showing all ink entries, witness initials, step timestamps, and field notes.

### 5. Calibrated Instrument Register
A complete traceability log listing every multimeter, power quality analyzer, ultrasonic flowmeter, digital thermometer, differential pressure transmitter, and thermal imaging camera deployed during testing. Embed copies of their ISO/IEC 17025 calibration certificates.

### 6. Raw Time-Series Data Repository
A structured archive containing the 1-second raw telemetry exports from the load banks, power meters, and BMS trend logs. To prevent post-test manipulation, generate a cryptographic hash (SHA-256 checksum) for every raw data file and record the hash table in the report appendix.

### 7. Resolved Master Issues Register
The final, printed copy of the Commissioning Issues Log. Every Category 1 and Category 2 defect must show its complete resolution history: initial finding, contractor remediation, witnessed re-test data sheet reference, and closeout signature. Any remaining open Category 3 cosmetic items must be bound by an approved 30-day closeout plan.

### 8. Systems Manual Operational Supplement
The operational bridge between commissioning data and daily facility operations. This section extracts critical baseline characteristics from the test data:
- The verified cold no-heat pump curve versus hot operating points (Sheet 6).
- Calibrated PID loop parameters for the primary modulating valve (TCV-101).
- The exact secondary fluid inventory (V_total) and glycol concentration (Refractometer verified 25.0% ± 0.5%).
- The emergency interlock logic matrix, defining hardware trip thresholds.

### 9. Operations Team Training Sign-Off
Documentation of formal operational handover training conducted with site facility engineers. Training must include physical walkthroughs of the emergency stop mechanisms, manual bypass valve operations, secondary fluid makeup procedures, and alarm acknowledgement workflows.

## The Final Page Boundary Statement

The final page of the report must protect the testing party and the owner by clearly stating what the verification did not cover:

| **FORMAL BOUNDARY STATEMENT** |
| :--- |
| "This verification campaign certifies the performance of the liquid cooling infrastructure under |
| simulated electrical and thermal load conditions as explicitly documented herein. It does not |
| certify the operational reliability, compute workload throughput, or warranty compliance of |
| production IT hardware. Systems marked as excluded or not demonstrated remain outside the scope |
| of this certification. All verified capacities are contingent upon the facility operating within |
| the environmental, electrical, and hydraulic boundaries established in this report." |

---

## 3. Field Verification Checklist and Instrumentation Hygiene

To execute this protocol without introducing measurement bias or scope ambiguity, the responsible engineer enforces four mandatory field rules:
1. **Instrument Traceability Before Observation**: Verify that every thermometer (4-wire Pt100 RTD Class A), pressure transducer ($\le \pm 0.1\%$ span), flowmeter, balometer, or power analyzer carries a current calibration certificate and passes a pre-test zero/span check on the day of the walk.
2. **Synchronized Time-Series Capture**: Align all digital loggers and gateway pollers to a single UTC reference clock (via IEEE 1588v2 PTP at $\pm 1\,\text{ms}$ for electrical Sequence of Events, or NTP at $\pm 10\,\text{ms}$ for thermal/hydraulic dwells). Never merge unsynchronized CSV files by row index.
3. **Explicit Isolation of Disturbances vs. Control Handles**: Hold upstream supply temperatures, parallel cabinet loads, and containment door states constant during the observation dwell so that transient plant drift is never mistaken for steady-state equipment performance.
4. **Written Record Prior to Signature**: Record every boundary tag, measured value, uncertainty tolerance, and open limitation in ink on the controlled project sheet before leaving the equipment line-up.

## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

### Why does "Close-out is not a heat-test report" matter during high-density data center commissioning and operations?
The seven mandatory deliverables required in a liquid cooling verification closeout binder—beyond a single thermal load bank chart. When project teams bypass this rule to meet a commercial schedule milestone, unverified physical assumptions—such as hidden hydraulic pressure drops, unlogged polling gaps, unblanked bypass leakage, or uncalibrated sensor offsets—transfer directly into live 24/7 production as latent single points of failure.

### How do you quantitatively verify compliance with "liquid cooling commissioning closeout package" on the physical floor?
Compliance is verified by executing the governing mathematical balance ($$\text{Closeout Pack} = \{\text{Claim}, \text{Level Map}, \text{Flash Judgment}, \text{Punch List}, \text{Witness Log}, \text{Ops Pages}, \text{Cal Certs}\}$$) using independent, calibrated field instruments across a stabilized steady-state dwell window (minimum 15 to 30 minutes for thermal and hydraulic systems), and confirming that the discrepancy between primary and secondary measurements remains strictly within the pre-declared acceptance band.

### What should an engineer do if a contractor or vendor submits a report that violates this protocol?
The reviewing engineer must refuse to sign the broad acceptance sentence, mark the specific line item as **Unproved / Defective** on the official audit sheet, and either require a witnessed re-test under a corrected script or isolate the unproved scope under a time-bounded Conditional Acceptance with a $150\%$ to $200\%$ financial retainage escrow holdback.

# One liquid system at a time: First-Principles Data Center Engineering Protocol

> **Direct Answer Block**: Why liquid cooling verification must execute static cleanliness flushes and zero-heat cold pump curves across every CDU and manifold before energizing load bank heaters. In mission-critical data center commissioning and operations, engineers enforce this boundary using deterministic physical equations, calibrated field instrumentation, and auditable sign-off gates rather than relying on vendor brochure summaries, uncalibrated software plots, or verbal assurances. Every measurement and state transition must be recorded with synchronized UTC timestamps and explicit pass/fail thresholds before a signature is granted.

![One system before the integrated heat window.](figures/flagship/fig-03-pump-curves-cold-vs-hot.png)

A liquid hall is more than one machine sharing pipes. If you heat the whole hall before one system has shown it can run, a failure has too many owners. The landed order that survives without site names is simple: survey, static checks, one system at a time, a no-heat pump curve, then the heat scripts, then shutdown, then the report.

The no-heat curve matters. It tells you the pumps and the path before energy confuses the picture. Skipping it because the schedule wants heat is how a flow problem is discovered as a temperature problem.

An open fail blocks the next stage. "We will watch it during heat" is not a close. It is a decision to run later with a known defect, and it needs a waiver that says what you will do if the defect appears under heat. A waiver without that sentence is permission to be surprised.

Do not mix a bad file with a plant fail. If the load bank file is not a valid test, that is not yet a punch item against the constructor. Separate the owners before you write the line.

---

## 1. First-Principles Engineering Formulation and Governing Mathematics

In high-density data center environments, verbal summaries and qualitative status tiles routinely obscure incipient physical failures. Whether auditing a $120\,\text{kW}$ liquid-cooled rack boundary, evaluating a 1-second telemetry time series, or verifying plant redundancy prior to handover, the governing physical relationship for this protocol is expressed as:

$$\Delta P_{\text{system}}(Q) = K_{\text{loop}} \cdot \rho(T) \cdot Q^2, \qquad \rho_{\text{PG25}}(20^\circ\text{C}) = 1030\,\text{kg/m}^3 \to \rho_{\text{PG25}}(45^\circ\text{C}) = 1018\,\text{kg/m}^3$$

When any term on the left-hand or right-hand side of this relationship is left unmeasured, inferred from an uncalibrated nameplate, or averaged across an unverified time window, the resulting engineering record cannot support a valid operational signature. Field engineers must verify each physical variable independently using NIST/ISO 17025 traceable instruments before proceeding to the next gate in the sequence.

| Audit Verification Parameter | Unacceptable / Defective Field Practice | Auditable First-Principles Requirement | Mandatory Action on Failure |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Boundary Definition** | Implied by vendor brochure or slide deck | Explicitly bounded on stamped P&ID / SLD with tag IDs | Halt acceptance; issue formal boundary clarification |
| **Measurement & Telemetry Proof** | Single uncalibrated display reading or 60-sec average | Calibrated Class A/0.5S sensor with 1-sec UTC timestamp | Reject dataset; classify point as `0x40` Stale or `0x80` Bad |
| **Pass / Fail Acceptance Gate** | Qualitative "Looks OK" or "Within Normal Range" | Quantitative numerical corridor cited from revision in force | Log Category A/B defect; withhold retainage or permit |
| **Custody & Sign-Off Record** | Single bundled "Accepted" signature at end of meeting | Scoped, dated sentence naming exact proved & unproved lines | Strike unsupported claims; issue Conditional Refusal |

---

## 2. Deep-Dive Technical Protocol and Field Implementation

The following field protocol—adapted directly from **Volume 03: *Finish a Liquid Cooling Verification: Seven Sheets for One Load-Bank Test***—establishes the step-by-step verification mechanics required on the data hall floor:

Dynamic verification with multiple interconnected systems under thermal load is a later, integrated phase. This phase is dedicated to validating one machine at a time, executing the precise operational logic defined in its standalone test script while all adjacent systems remain quiet.

In the global commissioning hierarchy, this is **Level 4 Functional Performance Testing (FPT)**. It validates the autonomous protection, modulating control loops, and physical alarms of individual machines before they are subjected to multi-megawatt thermal stress. Filing single-system testing under Level 5 Integrated Systems Testing simply because the equipment is physically located in the data hall is a serious documentation error.


## Autonomous Coolant Distribution Unit (CDU) Verification

The Coolant Distribution Unit is the critical hydraulic interface separating the facility primary water system (FWS) from the secondary technology cooling system (TCS). Before any thermal load is applied by the load banks, the CDU must prove its ability to control fluid circulation autonomously under Script 04 and Script 05.

### 1. Pump Startup, VFD Modulation, and Soft-Start
Energize the CDU secondary pumps with the primary facility loop isolated. Execute controlled start and stop cycles:
- Verify that the Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs) ramp the canned centrifugal pumps smoothly over their configured acceleration curve (typically 10 to 15 seconds) without causing electrical current spikes or hydraulic surges.
- Verify manual frequency override: drive the VFDs across their operating range (30.0 Hz to 50.0/60.0 Hz) and record motor current, power factor, and bearing vibration signatures.

### 2. N+1 Secondary Pump Auto-Changeover
Modern high-density CDUs employ an N+1 secondary pumping configuration (e.g., dual 100% capacity pumps, P-1A Lead and P-1B Standby). The automatic changeover logic must be verified through physical trip simulation:
- Operate Pump P-1A at 100% nominal speed with the loop at design operating flow.
- Simulate an electrical trip by opening the control circuit breaker to the P-1A inverter or triggering its digital fault input.
- **Acceptance Criteria**:
 - The local CDU controller must detect the fault, log a critical alarm, and issue a start command to standby Pump P-1B within ≤ 500 ms.
 - Standby Pump P-1B must accelerate to full operating speed and restore secondary differential pressure within ≤ 1.5 seconds.
 - The discharge non-return check valve on Pump P-1A must seat firmly without violent hydraulic slam (peak water hammer pulse must not exceed ± 50 kPa).
 - Secondary loop differential pressure must not drop below the minimum cavitation floor (100 kPa), ensuring continuous flow through the load banks without triggering false thermal trips.

### 3. Modulating Temperature Control Valve (TCV) Tracking
The primary loop Temperature Control Valve (TCV-101, typically a modulating 2-way or 3-way globe valve with an electronic actuator) regulates primary facility chilled water flow through the Plate Heat Exchanger (PHE-101) to maintain secondary supply temperature:
- Drive the actuator through its full control range using a 0–10V DC or 4–20 mA calibration source.
- Verify full-stroke opening and closing times against the manufacturer submittal (typically τ ≤ 30 seconds).
- Verify fail-safe position upon loss of control power: TCV-101 must fail mechanically open (100% primary flow) or hold last position depending on facility design intent.
- Verify seat leakage integrity: with the valve commanded 100% closed, confirm that primary flow drops to zero (leakage class ANSI/FCI 70-2 Class IV or better).

### 4. Secondary Differential Pressure Bypass Valve (BPV)
Inspect modulating bypass valve BPV-201, installed across secondary supply and return headers. Verify that as downstream manifold balancing valves are throttled, the BPV modulates open smoothly to maintain constant pump head, preventing impeller dead-heading.

## BMS Telemetry and Field Instrument Point-to-Point Checks

Never assume that a value displayed on a Building Management System (BMS) screen or CDU human-machine interface (HMI) reflects physical reality. Every telemetry point defined in the project claim must undergo physical point-to-point cross-checking against calibrated field reference instruments:

**POINT-TO-POINT TELEMETRY CALIBRATION AUDIT**

| TELEMETRY POINT | BMS / HMI READING | FIELD CALIBRATED REF | ALLOWABLE DELTA | AUDIT VERDICT |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Secondary Supply T | 40.12 °C | 40.08 °C (PT100) | +/- 0.30 K | PASS |
| Secondary Return T | 50.25 °C | 50.15 °C (PT100) | +/- 0.30 K | PASS |
| Secondary Flow Rate | 115.4 m³/h | 116.1 m³/h (Ultrason) | +/- 2.0% | PASS |
| Secondary Supply P | 285.0 kPa | 282.5 kPa (Gauge) | +/- 10.0 kPa | PASS |
| Secondary Return P | 115.0 kPa | 118.0 kPa (Gauge) | +/- 10.0 kPa | PASS |
| Expansion Tank Level | 68.0 % | 67.5 % (Sight Glass) | +/- 3.0 % | PASS |

If a discrepancy exceeds the allowable tolerance, the sensor offset must be recalibrated or the sensor replaced. Never adjust the acceptable tolerance band to match a drifting sensor.

## Physical Hardware Alarm Injection

Alarms must be validated through physical hardware injection. Simulating an alarm by altering a software setpoint in a configuration file or toggling a bit in an engineering workstation is completely unacceptable. Software simulation proves that software can read a variable; it does not prove that the physical sensor, field wiring, and relay logic function under real-world conditions.

Execute physical alarm testing under Script 06:
- **Secondary Low Flow Alarm**: Gradually throttle the manual isolation valve on the secondary supply header until the electromagnetic flowmeter registers flow dropping below the low-flow trip threshold. Confirm that the CDU controller sounds the local alarm horn, illuminates the red beacon, transmits an urgent Modbus/BACnet alarm to the central BMS, and trips the load-bank interlock relay.
- **Expansion Tank Low Liquid Level**: Manually depress the test lever on the expansion tank magnetic float switch. Verify that the CDU alerts the operator, locks out the electric heaters, and commands the automatic makeup water pump to start.
- **Secondary Loop Liquid Leak Detection**: Apply 5 mL of demineralized water across the external leak detection sensing rope positioned beneath the CDU piping connections and the manifold tray. Verify that the leak detection controller triggers within < 2.0 seconds, displays the exact leak distance location, and sends a critical latching alarm to the supervisory BMS.

**THREE POSSIBLE AUDIT VERDICTS FOR AN ALARM**

| 1. PASS | Alarm physically injected at sensor; local annunciator active; BMS logged event with correct timestamp and description; interlock executed cleanly. |
| :--- | :--- |
| 2. FAIL | Alarm injected but sensor failed to detect; delay exceeded tolerance; interlock relay failed to drop; logged immediately on Master Punch List. |
| 3. NOT DEMONSTRATED | Equipment lacks the physical sensor, wiring, or software register to raise this alarm. Explicitly logged as "NOT DEMONSTRATED" on Sheet 2. Never "PASS". |

If a specific alarm cannot be demonstrated because the hardware was omitted during construction, the line on Sheet 2 must be recorded as **NOT DEMONSTRATED**. Logging an untested alarm as "PASS" because "the vendor promised the logic works" is a serious professional breach.

## The Level 4 Prerequisite Gate

Level 4 functional performance testing concludes when all single-system scripts are fully executed and signed. Any failed alarm injection, uncalibrated sensor, or hunting control valve must be formally resolved and re-tested before the facility advances to multi-system thermal testing.

## PROTOCOL: Certificate Level 1 is not a static test

# Certificate Level 1 is not a static test

> **Direct Answer Block**: How to prevent numbering collisions between site test stages and ASHRAE Guideline 0 / Guideline 202 Commissioning Levels 1 through 5. In mission-critical data center commissioning and operations, engineers enforce this boundary using deterministic physical equations, calibrated field instrumentation, and auditable sign-off gates rather than relying on vendor brochure summaries, uncalibrated software plots, or verbal assurances. Every measurement and state transition must be recorded with synchronized UTC timestamps and explicit pass/fail thresholds before a signature is granted.

![Certificate Level 1 is factory testing.](figures/flagship/fig-04-multi-rack-manifold-hydraulics.png)

Commissioning certificates and site procedures often use the word level for different gates. In the certificate set, Level 1 is factory testing. Level 2 is delivery, installation, and pre-start. Functional testing and integrated testing sit later. Close-out is the last certificate, not the heat report.

A finished liquid hall often arrives with its own dialect. Static acceptance, no energy, gets called Level 1 because it is the first thing that team does on site. That label is locally clear and globally false. Drop the static report into the factory slot and you have certified a test you did not run.

Write both maps on the first page, in a table a tired person can read at the door. Static work sits with pre-start, not with the factory. One machine at a time, if it is a functional test, is not "Level 1" on anything that will be signed. The heat window, more than one system, is integrated testing. Calling it a local stage 3 is harmless only if the cover says so, and the certificate does not.

A note that design and factory acceptance were left out is allowed. Reusing the words Level 1 for a different gate is not.

---

## 1. First-Principles Engineering Formulation and Governing Mathematics

In high-density data center environments, verbal summaries and qualitative status tiles routinely obscure incipient physical failures. Whether auditing a $120\,\text{kW}$ liquid-cooled rack boundary, evaluating a 1-second telemetry time series, or verifying plant redundancy prior to handover, the governing physical relationship for this protocol is expressed as:

$$\text{ASHRAE Level } 1\,(\text{FAT}) \to \text{Level } 2\,(\text{QA/QC}) \to \text{Level } 3\,(\text{Pre-Start}) \to \text{Level } 4\,(\text{FPT}) \to \text{Level } 5\,(\text{IST})$$

When any term on the left-hand or right-hand side of this relationship is left unmeasured, inferred from an uncalibrated nameplate, or averaged across an unverified time window, the resulting engineering record cannot support a valid operational signature. Field engineers must verify each physical variable independently using NIST/ISO 17025 traceable instruments before proceeding to the next gate in the sequence.

| Audit Verification Parameter | Unacceptable / Defective Field Practice | Auditable First-Principles Requirement | Mandatory Action on Failure |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Boundary Definition** | Implied by vendor brochure or slide deck | Explicitly bounded on stamped P&ID / SLD with tag IDs | Halt acceptance; issue formal boundary clarification |
| **Measurement & Telemetry Proof** | Single uncalibrated display reading or 60-sec average | Calibrated Class A/0.5S sensor with 1-sec UTC timestamp | Reject dataset; classify point as `0x40` Stale or `0x80` Bad |
| **Pass / Fail Acceptance Gate** | Qualitative "Looks OK" or "Within Normal Range" | Quantitative numerical corridor cited from revision in force | Log Category A/B defect; withhold retainage or permit |
| **Custody & Sign-Off Record** | Single bundled "Accepted" signature at end of meeting | Scoped, dated sentence naming exact proved & unproved lines | Strike unsupported claims; issue Conditional Refusal |

## 2. Deep-Dive Technical Protocol and Field Implementation

The following field protocol—adapted directly from **Volume 03: *Finish a Liquid Cooling Verification: Seven Sheets for One Load-Bank Test***—establishes the step-by-step verification mechanics required on the data hall floor:

This chapter prevents an accurate site test report from being filed into an audit binder as fraudulent documentation.

In global mission-critical data center commissioning, documentation is structured around seven standard completion certificate tiers. Simultaneously, local mechanical contractors frequently communicate using a colloquial "three-stage" vocabulary. When these two vocabularies are carelessly conflated, audit compliance collapses.


## The Global Standard: Levels 0 Through 6

Modern commissioning frameworks (governed by ASHRAE Guideline 0-2019, ASHRAE Guideline 1.1, and the AABC Commissioning Group) define seven formal completion certificates:

- **Level 0: Design and Planning.** Audit of OPR, BOD, and engineering specifications. Certification that design intent and commissioning requirements are fully integrated.
- **Level 1: Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT).** Witnessed testing at the manufacturing plant (CDU vendor, chiller factory, load-bank fabricator). Validates pressure vessels, pump curves, and controls under factory conditions.
- **Level 2: Component Delivery, Receipt, and Static QA.** Uncrating, physical visual inspection, seismic anchoring verification, torque testing, and static de-energized electrical insulation checks.
- **Level 3: Pre-Functional Checks (PFC) and System Start-Up.** Chemical pipe flushing, hydrostatic pressure holds, vacuum deaeration, fluid charging, initial equipment energization, and manufacturer startup.
- **Level 4: Functional Performance Testing (FPT).** Dynamic testing of individual, isolated machines. Proves autonomous CDU pump sequencing, modulating valve response, local VFD control loops, and instrument point-to-point telemetry.
- **Level 5: Integrated System Testing (IST).** Multi-system dynamic verification under full simulated thermal heat. Verifies row-level manifold balance, multi-tier thermal steps, 2N power loss failover, primary cooling interruption ride-through, and emergency shutdown cascades.
- **Level 6: Close-Out, Turnover, and Operations Handover.** Resolution of all punch list items, final systems manual submission, operations team training, and handover to live site facilities engineering.

## The Local Dialect: Three Stages

On a retrofit project or a completed hall where a liquid verification team is mobilized specifically for a load-bank campaign, contractors routinely use an informal three-stage shorthand:
- **Stage 1: Static Acceptance (No Energy).** Physical installation, cable checks, hose connections, and pressure holds.
- **Stage 2: Single-System Function.** Individual CDU startup, pump rotation, and local alarms.
- **Stage 3: Integrated Thermal Performance.** Energizing the load banks, stepping through heat, and simulating facility power drops.

The stage sequence itself is logically sound: you do not energize equipment that has not passed static inspection, and you do not apply thermal load to a loop whose pumps have not been functionally proven. The hazard lies in the numbering.

## The Compliance Trap

Contractors frequently label their Stage 1 static walk-through as "Level 1 Testing" in project folders. When an auditor or client compliance officer reviews the project binders, they open the tab marked "Level 1: Factory Acceptance Testing" and discover a clipboard checklist verifying that secondary hoses were unboxed and clamped to a manifold.

Filing a site walk-through into a factory acceptance binder is documentation fraud. Even if every checkbox on that site checklist represents diligent physical work, the certificate is invalid because Level 1 requires factory test bench data, factory calibration sheets, and manufacturing witness signatures.

To prevent this compliance breach, the first page of the Commissioning Plan must feature a prominent cross-reference matrix:

**COMMISSIONING TIER TRANSLATION MATRIX**

| GLOBAL CERTIFICATE TIER | LOCAL FIELD CONTRACTOR TERM | MANDATORY VERIFICATION BOUNDARY |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Level 0: Design Audit | Excluded / Attached | OPR & BOD sign-off; design review waiver. |
| Level 1: Factory Testing | FAT Vendor Documentation | Factory test records attached as evidence. |
| Level 2: Site Receipt QA | Stage 1 (Static Part A) | Sheet 1: Unpack, megger, phase rotation. |
| Level 3: PFC & Start-Up | Stage 1 (Static Part B) | Sheet 1: Flush, hydro-hold, fill and vent. |
| Level 4: Functional (FPT) | Stage 2 (Single System) | Sheet 2, Sheet 6, Sheet 7: CDU & alarms. |
| Level 5: Integrated (IST) | Stage 3 (Heat Window) | Sheet 3, Sheet 4: Thermal ladder & 2N pull. |
| Level 6: Turnover | Closeout Handover | Sheet 5, Punch list clearance, Cx pack. |

## Mandatory Gating and Interlock Rules

A core tenet of commissioning governance is that no project may advance across a level boundary while unresolved defects exist in the preceding tier:

1. **Static Prerequisite Gate**: Level 4 Functional Performance Testing cannot commence if Level 3 Pre-Functional Checklists remain unsigned. Operating a CDU pump through an unverified, un-flushed secondary loop risks circulating metal shavings and construction debris directly into plate heat exchangers and quick disconnect valves.
2. **Thermal Prerequisite Gate**: Level 5 Integrated System Testing cannot commence if Level 4 single-system safety trips or pump changeover routines have failed. Introducing megawatts of thermal energy into a system with an unverified N+1 pump changeover guarantees an uncontrolled thermal runaway when a pump inevitably trips.
3. **The "Fix It During Heat" Trap**: When a contractor pleads, "Let us proceed with the heat test today and we will resolve the pump changeover issue tomorrow," the Commissioning Lead must issue an immediate stop. Thermal energy does not rectify mechanical and electrical defects; it magnifies them under high risk.

If an owner chooses to waive an open defect to maintain an aggressive project schedule, that waiver must be documented as a formal written deviation signed in ink by the Owner’s Project Engineer. The waiver must explicitly define the compensatory safety controls deployed on site. An informal verbal agreement is completely invalid.

## 3. Field Verification Checklist and Instrumentation Hygiene

To execute this protocol without introducing measurement bias or scope ambiguity, the responsible engineer enforces four mandatory field rules:
1. **Instrument Traceability Before Observation**: Verify that every thermometer (4-wire Pt100 RTD Class A), pressure transducer ($\le \pm 0.1\%$ span), flowmeter, balometer, or power analyzer carries a current calibration certificate and passes a pre-test zero/span check on the day of the walk.
2. **Synchronized Time-Series Capture**: Align all digital loggers and gateway pollers to a single UTC reference clock (via IEEE 1588v2 PTP at $\pm 1\,\text{ms}$ for electrical Sequence of Events, or NTP at $\pm 10\,\text{ms}$ for thermal/hydraulic dwells). Never merge unsynchronized CSV files by row index.
3. **Explicit Isolation of Disturbances vs. Control Handles**: Hold upstream supply temperatures, parallel cabinet loads, and containment door states constant during the observation dwell so that transient plant drift is never mistaken for steady-state equipment performance.
4. **Written Record Prior to Signature**: Record every boundary tag, measured value, uncertainty tolerance, and open limitation in ink on the controlled project sheet before leaving the equipment line-up.

## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

### Why does "Certificate Level 1 is not a static test" matter during high-density data center commissioning and operations?
How to prevent numbering collisions between site test stages and ASHRAE Guideline 0 / Guideline 202 Commissioning Levels 1 through 5. When project teams bypass this rule to meet a commercial schedule milestone, unverified physical assumptions—such as hidden hydraulic pressure drops, unlogged polling gaps, unblanked bypass leakage, or uncalibrated sensor offsets—transfer directly into live 24/7 production as latent single points of failure.

### How do you quantitatively verify compliance with "ASHRAE Guideline 0 commissioning levels 1 to 5" on the physical floor?
Compliance is verified by executing the governing mathematical balance ($$\text{ASHRAE Level } 1\,(\text{FAT}) \to \text{Level } 2\,(\text{QA/QC}) \to \text{Level } 3\,(\text{Pre-Start}) \to \text{Level } 4\,(\text{FPT}) \to \text{Level } 5\,(\text{IST})$$) using independent, calibrated field instruments across a stabilized steady-state dwell window (minimum 15 to 30 minutes for thermal and hydraulic systems), and confirming that the discrepancy between primary and secondary measurements remains strictly within the pre-declared acceptance band.

### What should an engineer do if a contractor or vendor submits a report that violates this protocol?
The reviewing engineer must refuse to sign the broad acceptance sentence, mark the specific line item as **Unproved / Defective** on the official audit sheet, and either require a witnessed re-test under a corrected script or isolate the unproved scope under a time-bounded Conditional Acceptance with a $150\%$ to $200\%$ financial retainage escrow holdback.

# What data center commissioning levels 0 to 6 sign

> **Direct Answer Block**: Complete technical breakdown of data center commissioning Levels 0 through 6: design review, FAT, static QA/QC, energizing, FPT, integrated IST, and handover. In mission-critical data center commissioning and operations, engineers enforce this boundary using deterministic physical equations, calibrated field instrumentation, and auditable sign-off gates rather than relying on vendor brochure summaries, uncalibrated software plots, or verbal assurances. Every measurement and state transition must be recorded with synchronized UTC timestamps and explicit pass/fail thresholds before a signature is granted.

![Seven certificate levels. The local dialect is not Level 1.](figures/flagship/fig-05-thermal-ladder-and-dwell.png)

People search for the seven levels and then file the wrong PDF in the slot. The certificate set is a map of what was concluded, not a mood.

Level 0 is design and planning, concluded. Level 1 is factory testing. Level 2 is delivery, installation, and pre-start. Level 3 is pre-functional checks and system start-up. Level 4 is functional testing of a system. Level 5 is integrated testing, more than one system. Level 6 is close-out and turnover. A heat-test report is not Level 6. Turnover is the later signature, after the punch on the levels you actually ran is closed, and after the map says which levels you did not run.

A finished hall often brings a second numbering. Its "Level 1" is static acceptance, no energy, because that was the first gate on site. That dialect can live in a procedure note. It must not be dropped into the factory certificate slot. Static work sits with pre-start, not with Level 1. One machine, if the script is a functional test, is Level 4 in the certificate pack. The heat window is Level 5. Close-out is Level 6, and only when the words on the page match the map.

A note that design and factory acceptance were left out is allowed. Silence is not a pass. If the map does not list a level as refused, the next reader will assume it was signed. Write the refusals on the first page.

Do not paste a certificate template into a public note. The titles are enough. Your file keeps the forms.

## 1. First-Principles Engineering Formulation and Governing Mathematics

In high-density data center environments, verbal summaries and qualitative status tiles routinely obscure incipient physical failures. Whether auditing a $120\,\text{kW}$ liquid-cooled rack boundary, evaluating a 1-second telemetry time series, or verifying plant redundancy prior to handover, the governing physical relationship for this protocol is expressed as:

$$\text{Gate}_{L(k)} = 1 \iff \text{Gate}_{L(k-1)} = 1 \;\land\; \text{Open Category A Defects} = 0$$

When any term on the left-hand or right-hand side of this relationship is left unmeasured, inferred from an uncalibrated nameplate, or averaged across an unverified time window, the resulting engineering record cannot support a valid operational signature. Field engineers must verify each physical variable independently using NIST/ISO 17025 traceable instruments before proceeding to the next gate in the sequence.

| Audit Verification Parameter | Unacceptable / Defective Field Practice | Auditable First-Principles Requirement | Mandatory Action on Failure |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Boundary Definition** | Implied by vendor brochure or slide deck | Explicitly bounded on stamped P&ID / SLD with tag IDs | Halt acceptance; issue formal boundary clarification |
| **Measurement & Telemetry Proof** | Single uncalibrated display reading or 60-sec average | Calibrated Class A/0.5S sensor with 1-sec UTC timestamp | Reject dataset; classify point as `0x40` Stale or `0x80` Bad |
| **Pass / Fail Acceptance Gate** | Qualitative "Looks OK" or "Within Normal Range" | Quantitative numerical corridor cited from revision in force | Log Category A/B defect; withhold retainage or permit |
| **Custody & Sign-Off Record** | Single bundled "Accepted" signature at end of meeting | Scoped, dated sentence naming exact proved & unproved lines | Strike unsupported claims; issue Conditional Refusal |

## 2. Deep-Dive Technical Protocol and Field Implementation

The following field protocol—adapted directly from **Volume 03: *Finish a Liquid Cooling Verification: Seven Sheets for One Load-Bank Test***—establishes the step-by-step verification mechanics required on the data hall floor:

This chapter prevents an accurate site test report from being filed into an audit binder as fraudulent documentation.

In global mission-critical data center commissioning, documentation is structured around seven standard completion certificate tiers. Simultaneously, local mechanical contractors frequently communicate using a colloquial "three-stage" vocabulary. When these two vocabularies are carelessly conflated, audit compliance collapses.


## The Global Standard: Levels 0 Through 6

Modern commissioning frameworks (governed by ASHRAE Guideline 0-2019, ASHRAE Guideline 1.1, and the AABC Commissioning Group) define seven formal completion certificates:

- **Level 0: Design and Planning.** Audit of OPR, BOD, and engineering specifications. Certification that design intent and commissioning requirements are fully integrated.
- **Level 1: Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT).** Witnessed testing at the manufacturing plant (CDU vendor, chiller factory, load-bank fabricator). Validates pressure vessels, pump curves, and controls under factory conditions.
- **Level 2: Component Delivery, Receipt, and Static QA.** Uncrating, physical visual inspection, seismic anchoring verification, torque testing, and static de-energized electrical insulation checks.
- **Level 3: Pre-Functional Checks (PFC) and System Start-Up.** Chemical pipe flushing, hydrostatic pressure holds, vacuum deaeration, fluid charging, initial equipment energization, and manufacturer startup.
- **Level 4: Functional Performance Testing (FPT).** Dynamic testing of individual, isolated machines. Proves autonomous CDU pump sequencing, modulating valve response, local VFD control loops, and instrument point-to-point telemetry.
- **Level 5: Integrated System Testing (IST).** Multi-system dynamic verification under full simulated thermal heat. Verifies row-level manifold balance, multi-tier thermal steps, 2N power loss failover, primary cooling interruption ride-through, and emergency shutdown cascades.
- **Level 6: Close-Out, Turnover, and Operations Handover.** Resolution of all punch list items, final systems manual submission, operations team training, and handover to live site facilities engineering.

## The Local Dialect: Three Stages

On a retrofit project or a completed hall where a liquid verification team is mobilized specifically for a load-bank campaign, contractors routinely use an informal three-stage shorthand:
- **Stage 1: Static Acceptance (No Energy).** Physical installation, cable checks, hose connections, and pressure holds.
- **Stage 2: Single-System Function.** Individual CDU startup, pump rotation, and local alarms.
- **Stage 3: Integrated Thermal Performance.** Energizing the load banks, stepping through heat, and simulating facility power drops.

The stage sequence itself is logically sound: you do not energize equipment that has not passed static inspection, and you do not apply thermal load to a loop whose pumps have not been functionally proven. The hazard lies in the numbering.

## The Compliance Trap

Contractors frequently label their Stage 1 static walk-through as "Level 1 Testing" in project folders. When an auditor or client compliance officer reviews the project binders, they open the tab marked "Level 1: Factory Acceptance Testing" and discover a clipboard checklist verifying that secondary hoses were unboxed and clamped to a manifold.

Filing a site walk-through into a factory acceptance binder is documentation fraud. Even if every checkbox on that site checklist represents diligent physical work, the certificate is invalid because Level 1 requires factory test bench data, factory calibration sheets, and manufacturing witness signatures.

To prevent this compliance breach, the first page of the Commissioning Plan must feature a prominent cross-reference matrix:

**COMMISSIONING TIER TRANSLATION MATRIX**

| GLOBAL CERTIFICATE TIER | LOCAL FIELD CONTRACTOR TERM | MANDATORY VERIFICATION BOUNDARY |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Level 0: Design Audit | Excluded / Attached | OPR & BOD sign-off; design review waiver. |
| Level 1: Factory Testing | FAT Vendor Documentation | Factory test records attached as evidence. |
| Level 2: Site Receipt QA | Stage 1 (Static Part A) | Sheet 1: Unpack, megger, phase rotation. |
| Level 3: PFC & Start-Up | Stage 1 (Static Part B) | Sheet 1: Flush, hydro-hold, fill and vent. |
| Level 4: Functional (FPT) | Stage 2 (Single System) | Sheet 2, Sheet 6, Sheet 7: CDU & alarms. |
| Level 5: Integrated (IST) | Stage 3 (Heat Window) | Sheet 3, Sheet 4: Thermal ladder & 2N pull. |
| Level 6: Turnover | Closeout Handover | Sheet 5, Punch list clearance, Cx pack. |

## Mandatory Gating and Interlock Rules

A core tenet of commissioning governance is that no project may advance across a level boundary while unresolved defects exist in the preceding tier:

1. **Static Prerequisite Gate**: Level 4 Functional Performance Testing cannot commence if Level 3 Pre-Functional Checklists remain unsigned. Operating a CDU pump through an unverified, un-flushed secondary loop risks circulating metal shavings and construction debris directly into plate heat exchangers and quick disconnect valves.
2. **Thermal Prerequisite Gate**: Level 5 Integrated System Testing cannot commence if Level 4 single-system safety trips or pump changeover routines have failed. Introducing megawatts of thermal energy into a system with an unverified N+1 pump changeover guarantees an uncontrolled thermal runaway when a pump inevitably trips.
3. **The "Fix It During Heat" Trap**: When a contractor pleads, "Let us proceed with the heat test today and we will resolve the pump changeover issue tomorrow," the Commissioning Lead must issue an immediate stop. Thermal energy does not rectify mechanical and electrical defects; it magnifies them under high risk.

If an owner chooses to waive an open defect to maintain an aggressive project schedule, that waiver must be documented as a formal written deviation signed in ink by the Owner’s Project Engineer. The waiver must explicitly define the compensatory safety controls deployed on site. An informal verbal agreement is completely invalid.

## PROTOCOL: Witnessed is not the same as accepted a document
- Canonical URL: https://datacenterfieldguides.com/blog/witnessed-or-a-document
- Raw Markdown URL: https://datacenterfieldguides.com/raw/witnessed-or-a-document.md

# Witnessed is not the same as accepted a document

> **Direct Answer Block**: Why commissioning certificates must explicitly distinguish between physical tests witnessed live on the data hall floor and vendor documents accepted at a desk. In mission-critical data center commissioning and operations, engineers enforce this boundary using deterministic physical equations, calibrated field instrumentation, and auditable sign-off gates rather than relying on vendor brochure summaries, uncalibrated software plots, or verbal assurances. Every measurement and state transition must be recorded with synchronized UTC timestamps and explicit pass/fail thresholds before a signature is granted.

![Witnessed, accepted as a document, or not done.](figures/flagship/fig-06-transient-failure-scenarios.png)

For each script someone wants called proved, the pack says which verb applies. Witnessed means a person saw the step. Accepted as a document means a paper was filed and a named party took it as the record. Not done means not done. A fourth word, "substantially complete," means not done, wearing a better coat. Do not add it.

If you cannot tell the verbs apart, you do not sign the proved sentence for that script. A document can be honest and still not be a witness. A missing witness does not make the document disappear. The signature has to say which one you are relying on.

A letter that says a setting was adjusted is not a witnessed changeover. A photograph of a label is not a leak test. A remote note that a value "looked normal" is not a file judgment. If a punch line was closed on one of these, do not inherit the close when the script asked for a witness the first time.

Sampling belongs in the same place. If every line was not witnessed, the pack says what was sampled and what rule picked the sample. "We saw enough" is not a rule. A sample can support a sentence about the sample. It cannot support a sentence about the hall. Strike the hall-wide claim.

A path a second person cannot open is not a document. You are relying on a name. Names are not records.

## 1. First-Principles Engineering Formulation and Governing Mathematics

In high-density data center environments, verbal summaries and qualitative status tiles routinely obscure incipient physical failures. Whether auditing a $120\,\text{kW}$ liquid-cooled rack boundary, evaluating a 1-second telemetry time series, or verifying plant redundancy prior to handover, the governing physical relationship for this protocol is expressed as:

$$N_{\text{witnessed}}(\text{Level 4/5}) = 100\%, \qquad N_{\text{sample}}(\text{Level 2/3}) \ge \lceil\sqrt{N}\rceil + 1$$

When any term on the left-hand or right-hand side of this relationship is left unmeasured, inferred from an uncalibrated nameplate, or averaged across an unverified time window, the resulting engineering record cannot support a valid operational signature. Field engineers must verify each physical variable independently using NIST/ISO 17025 traceable instruments before proceeding to the next gate in the sequence.

| Audit Verification Parameter | Unacceptable / Defective Field Practice | Auditable First-Principles Requirement | Mandatory Action on Failure |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Boundary Definition** | Implied by vendor brochure or slide deck | Explicitly bounded on stamped P&ID / SLD with tag IDs | Halt acceptance; issue formal boundary clarification |
| **Measurement & Telemetry Proof** | Single uncalibrated display reading or 60-sec average | Calibrated Class A/0.5S sensor with 1-sec UTC timestamp | Reject dataset; classify point as `0x40` Stale or `0x80` Bad |
| **Pass / Fail Acceptance Gate** | Qualitative "Looks OK" or "Within Normal Range" | Quantitative numerical corridor cited from revision in force | Log Category A/B defect; withhold retainage or permit |
